title: First Sleep Score with contributors
what: A big 73 with the word GOOD, a heading that says Your first Sleep Score, a short explainer, then a Contributors list with thin bars for total sleep, efficiency, restfulness and REM.
takeaway: Mark the very first score as a moment and explain the score right there, before the user has to look for help.

title: Sleep Fitness Score with weighted contributors
what: A half gauge reading 86 In range, with three contributor cards for time slept, quality and consistency, each tagged with its share of the score (40%, 50%, 10%) and a progress bar.
takeaway: Showing each contributor's weight as a small tag tells people what matters most without a separate explainer.

title: Sleep Index with stage timeline
what: A week strip of Sleep Index bars with today at 84, then a stage list with times and percentages and a hypnogram of awake, REM, light and deep across the night.
takeaway: A stage list with plain durations above the hypnogram gives the answer first and the detail second.

title: Schedule with optimal range band
what: Seven day floating bars from sleep to wake, with green dotted bands for the optimal bedtime and wake time, and 7-day averages labelled In range or Out of range (plus or minus 30 min).
takeaway: A simple plus or minus 30 minute window turns consistency into a yes or no that anyone can read.

title: Bedtime over past weeks, hit or miss
what: Bedtime bars over four weeks against a dotted ideal bedtime window, coloured as Hit or Miss, followed by a How can I find a consistent bedtime tip.
takeaway: Pairing the timing chart with one practical tip (start with a steady wake time) makes regularity something to act on.

title: Sleep Consistency chart
what: A 7-day chart of sleep times as vertical bars with a solid line for average bedtime and a dashed line for average wake time, plus the averages written out below.
takeaway: Average bedtime and wake time as two reference lines is the simplest regularity view, and it still works with only a few nights logged.

title: Weekly Sleep Score summary
what: A weekly report that opens with a sentence giving last week's average score of 78, seven score bars, and a note that scores over 70 mean a good night and 85 means excellent.
takeaway: Lead a weekly view with one sentence and state the thresholds in words so the bars mean something.

title: No Sleep Score yet
what: A moon icon with No Sleep Score yet and a line saying the score appears when the first analysis is ready, with the full contributor list shown below as empty rows.
takeaway: Showing the empty contributor list previews what the score will contain, so the waiting state still teaches.

title: HRV Status calibrating
what: An empty gauge with dashes and No Status, telling the user to wear the device while sleeping for about 3 weeks, while raw nightly values are still shown below.
takeaway: Say exactly how long until the score unlocks and still show the raw numbers collected so far.

title: No sleep animal this month
what: A No sleep animal message for the month explaining that 14 nights are needed, followed by a list of sleep animals like The Bear (solid sleeper) and The Dolphin (segmented sleeper).
takeaway: A friendly sleeper type gives people something to look forward to, and the empty state states the exact number of nights needed.

title: Readiness explainer
what: An onboarding style page with a ring illustration, the headline Readiness measures how recovered your body is, a 0 to 100 range, and short icon rows on what goes into it.
takeaway: Explain a new score once, in a full page with one headline and three short rows, before showing the number.

title: Readiness bands and what's a good score
what: Four named bands (Primed, Ready, Fatigued, Recovering) with number ranges and one line each, then a What's a good score section saying there is no good or bad score.
takeaway: Name each band with a word and a one line meaning, and say plainly that a low score is not a failure.

title: Coach note on shifting sleep timing
what: A coach message headed Your sleep timing is shifting quite a bit, explaining a bedtime that varied by over an hour and asking about a 10:00 PM lights-out, with score and sleep cards and a Reply button.
takeaway: A coach line can pick the one thing that matters (timing, not the high score) and end with a question the user can answer.

title: Sleep Score with plain headline
what: A score of 84 with Good quality and 6h 55m, a headline Shorter than ideal, restorative, two short sentences of explanation, and a collapsed Sleep Score Factors section.
takeaway: A two part headline (what was short, what went well) explains a mixed night better than a single word.

title: Morning Stability with score summary
what: A small gauge reading 4 with Looking stable and a reassuring line, then a Your score summary list where each row is a full sentence about HRV, resting heart rate and sleep compared with the user's own baseline.
takeaway: Writing each contributor as a full sentence against the person's own normal reads well for older users who do not know the metrics.

title: Sleep debt home
what: A large 0.2 hrs Sleep debt figure on a curved card with a GREAT for 11 days badge, change since yesterday, Energy Potential 99%, and a Next up Melatonin window card.
takeaway: One number in hours plus the next timed action (a wind-down window) is easier to act on than a 0 to 100 score.

title: Sleep summary with Sleep Score card
what: The Sleep page with a Time Asleep card and a Sleep Score card that reads High, 84 points with a small segmented ring.
takeaway: The entry card leads with the word band (High) and keeps the number secondary.

title: Sleep Score with point breakdown
what: A card with High and a segmented ring at 84, showing Duration 40/50, Bedtime 24/30 and Interruptions 20/20, with one sentence on why the score came out at 84.
takeaway: Points out of a fixed total per contributor (50, 30, 20) make the sum readable and show where the missing points went.

title: Sleep Score detail with per-part notes
what: The score detail for a date with each part listed with its points and a short note, like Not enough REM and Deep, Expected: 8:00 AM, and No wake-ups.
takeaway: A three to five word note under each part tells the user why without opening another screen.

title: About Sleep Score
what: A plain text explainer describing the five quality levels (Excellent to Very Low), what goes into the score, and a note that it is not a measure of how you feel.
takeaway: An honest explainer that says what the score is not builds trust, and fits at the bottom of the detail page.

title: Home with three score rings
what: The home screen with Sleep 69%, Recovery 86% and Strain 5.5 rings side by side, and an Elevated HRV insight card below.
takeaway: Pillar scores as a row of rings on home, each tappable into its own breakdown, is a clear entry pattern.

title: Sleep Performance with contributors
what: A ring at 69% Sleep Performance with rows for hours vs needed, consistency, efficiency and high sleep stress, each with a Poor, Sufficient or Optimal bar, and an AI note card at the bottom.
takeaway: A three level legend per contributor is simpler than many numbers, and the AI note sits right under the breakdown.

title: Last night's sleep with typical range
what: Hours of sleep with a heart rate trace, then awake, light, deep and REM bars each shaded against the user's typical range, with an AI note saying the night was limited by time asleep more than quality.
takeaway: Comparing each stage to the user's own typical range, plus one sentence naming the main cause, answers why the score moved.

title: Weekly hours vs needed and restorative sleep
what: A week of bars showing hours vs needed as a percentage each night, and a stacked bar chart of deep and REM hours below.
takeaway: Showing sleep as a percent of what you needed makes a weekly view fair across short and long nights.

title: Sleep trends list with normal range tags
what: A list of trend cards for Sleep Score, Time Asleep, REM, Deep, Heart Rate Dip and Sleep Bank, each with a value, a Normal range or Debt tag, and a tiny sparkline.
takeaway: A status tag against the user's own normal range on every card makes a long metric list scannable.

title: Sleep Score trend with personal range
what: A bottom sheet showing 67% with Normal range 43 to 82, a one month line chart with a shaded personal range and a dotted average of 62%, and 1M, 3M, 6M, 1Y toggles.
takeaway: A shaded personal range behind the trend line shows whether today is normal for this person, not for everyone.

title: Sleep breakdown bands and trend analysis
what: A segmented bar defining Low, Normal and Optimal bands, then a table of change over 3, 7, 14, 30 and 90 days with arrows and mini trend lines.
takeaway: Spelling out band cutoffs and change over several windows helps a coach see direction at a glance.
